deep.reconstruction:
The page has five separate entries. The number-theoretic plan fits about 1898–1900, the period of Hilbert's papers on relative-quadratic and relative-abelian fields and of the 1900 Paris problems. The Molien remark may be later (see entry D).

(A) 'Plan für meine künftigen zahlentheoretischen Studien' (no computation).
(1) Generalize the theory of relative-quadratic fields K(√μ)/K to relative-abelian (cyclic) extensions of prime relative degree l. Work out in full the special case of a field that is relatively cubic over a quadratic field.
(2) Push the general theory far enough to prove Fermat's theorem x^l + y^l + z^l = 0 in general, i.e. a Kummer-type programme via class fields.
(3) Push the theory of relative-abelian fields far enough to apply it to complex multiplication and modular functions. This is the programme of Hilbert's 12th problem, Kronecker's Jugendtraum.
One struck-out item, overwritten in black and blue ink, lies between items 2 and 3.

(B) 'Beweise den Satz' (a statement to prove).
Let K be the field generated by the coefficients and f = Σ a_ij x_i x_j a quadratic form in 5 variables over K. Claim: if f is indefinite in every real field conjugate to K, then f = 0 has a nontrivial solution in K.
Modern form: a quinary quadratic form over a number field is isotropic iff it is isotropic at all real places. Every nondegenerate form in at least 5 variables is isotropic over every non-archimedean completion, so this follows from the Hasse–Minkowski theorem.
The follow-up heading 'Kriterien für die Transformirbarkeit quadratischer Formen' is the equivalence problem: when are two forms equivalent (over K or over its integers)? That is the content of Hilbert's 11th problem.

(C) A conjectured local-global principle.
'Eine Gl. 3ten oder 4ten Grades ist in einem Rationalitätsbereiche stets lösbar, wenn sie nach jedem Modul als Congruenz aufgefaßt lösbar ist.' In words: an equation of degree 3 or 4 is solvable in the number field if it is solvable as a congruence modulo every modulus.
Reading (i), a homogeneous Diophantine equation (form) of degree 3 or 4 in several variables, the natural continuation of (B): the claim is false.
- Cubic counterexample: Selmer (1951), 3x^3 + 4y^3 + 5z^3 = 0. It is solvable modulo every n and over R, but has no nontrivial rational solution.
- Quartic counterexamples: Lind (1940) and Reichardt (1942), e.g. 2y^2 = x^4 − 17.
Reading (ii), a polynomial in one unknown of degree 3 or 4: the claim is true. A root modulo every prime (ideal) forces a root in K.
- An irreducible polynomial of degree > 1 has no root modulo infinitely many primes (Jordan/Frobenius–Chebotarev).
- A product of two irreducible quadratics also fails at infinitely many primes.
- A reducible cubic, or a quartic with a linear factor, already has a rational root.
- The first counterexamples have degree 5, e.g. (x^2+3)(x^3−2).
The restriction to degree 3 or 4 fits reading (ii); the context fits reading (i).

(D) Bibliographic remark.
T. Molien, 'Ueber Systeme höherer complexer Zahlen', Math. Ann. 41 (1893). Hilbert notes that it 'contains everything Frobenius has done, shorter and better'. The comparison is with Frobenius's work on hypercomplex numbers (1903), and possibly his group determinant and character work (1896–99).

(E) AM–GM by forward–backward induction (Hilbert credits Hurwitz). Claim: for a_i > 0, (a_1+…+a_n)/n ≥ (a_1⋯a_n)^{1/n}.
Step 1 (on this page): if true for n, then true for 2n.
- Let G1 = (a_1⋯a_n)^{1/n} and G2 = (a_{n+1}⋯a_{2n})^{1/n}.
- By hypothesis (a_1+…+a_n)/n ≥ G1 and (a_{n+1}+…+a_{2n})/n ≥ G2.
- Adding: (a_1+…+a_{2n})/n ≥ G1 + G2.
- By the n = 2 case (implicit, my filling): G1 + G2 ≥ 2√(G1 G2) = 2(a_1⋯a_{2n})^{1/(2n)}.
- Dividing by 2 gives the 2n case. q.e.d.
- Implicit base (mine): n = 2 holds because (√a − √b)^2 ≥ 0. Hence AM–GM holds for all powers of 2.
Step 2 (next page): if true for n, then true for n−1.
- Let A = (a_1+…+a_{n−1})/(n−1) and apply the n case to a_1,…,a_{n−1},A.
- The mean of these n numbers is ((n−1)A + A)/n = A.
- So A ≥ (a_1⋯a_{n−1}·A)^{1/n}, i.e. A^n ≥ a_1⋯a_{n−1}·A.
- Hence A^{n−1} ≥ a_1⋯a_{n−1}. A stray factor n/(n−1) was written and struck out. q.e.d.
The two steps together give the inequality for all n.
errors: AM-GM step 1 silently uses the n=2 case (G1+G2 ≥ 2√(G1G2)) and the base case is not stated. This is harmless.
In the n→n−1 step on the next page an erroneous factor n/(n−1) was written and then struck out by Hilbert. The final inequality is correct.

Entry C, if read as a statement about homogeneous Diophantine equations (cubic or quartic forms or curves), is false: Selmer's 3x^3+4y^3+5z^3=0 (1951) and the Lind–Reichardt quartic 2y^2=x^4−17. Even as stated it omits the real (archimedean) condition that entry B includes. Read as a one-variable polynomial statement, it is true.
Entry B omits the obvious nondegeneracy or nontrivial-solution qualifiers. These are standard and implicit.

The attribution of the forward–backward induction proof of AM–GM to Hurwitz is historically inaccurate. The method is Cauchy's (Cours d'analyse, 1821). Hurwitz's 1891 Crelle paper gives a different proof via symmetric polynomials. Hilbert may simply have learned it from Hurwitz.

deep.surprise_reason: Most of the page is routine: a research plan matching Hilbert's known programme and the 12th problem, a textbook AM–GM proof, and a bibliographic remark. Two entries are mildly notable. The first is an explicit note to prove the quinary-form theorem over arbitrary number fields, i.e. Meyer's theorem over number fields, later proved by Hasse; this fits Hilbert's 11th problem and his norm-residue work, so it is consistent with known interests. The second is an explicit local-global conjecture for degree 3 and 4, which is false for forms and was refuted only in 1940–51, if that is the intended reading. Hilbert's frank preference for Molien over Frobenius is a small historical curiosity.

Base case n=2 of AM–GM, with x=√G1, y=√G2: (G1+G2)/2 − √(G1G2) = (√G1−√G2)^2/2 ≥ 0 (result 0).

Example of the quinary statement: the indefinite form x1^2+x2^2+x3^2+x4^2−7x5^2 has a nontrivial rational zero (result 0).

checkable.asserts: Selmer's cubic has nontrivial solutions modulo small primes (local solvability), even though it has no nontrivial rational solution. This counters reading (i) of entry C.

checkable.asserts: The irreducible quartic x^4−2 has no root modulo infinitely many primes (e.g. 5, 13, 29, …). This illustrates why reading (ii) of entry C holds for one-variable polynomials.

checkable.sympy: all(any(((x**2+3)*(x**3-2))%p==0 for x in range(p)) for p in primerange(2,200))
checkable.asserts: (x^2+3)(x^3−2) has a root modulo every prime but no rational root; degree 5 is the first degree where the one-variable local-global statement fails.

transcription_corrections: Molien's paper is titled 'Ueber Systeme höherer complexer Zahlen' (Math. Ann. 41, 1893). Hilbert's note abbreviates it as 'Ueber Systeme complexer Zahlen'.

Item 1 of the plan reads approximately: 'Die Sätze über den relativquadratischen Körper auf den relativ-abelschen Körper vom Relativgrade l übertragen allgemein und in dem besonderen Falle der Körper welcher relativ cubisch in Bezug auf einen quadratischen ist ausführlich beweisen'. The struck words are 'vom' and 'dem fol..'.
The right-hand side of the Fermat equation in item 2 is cramped and uncertain in the image; it may be '=0' or '=1'. The intended statement is Fermat's Last Theorem for exponent l in either case.
Below item 2 a whole line is struck out in black and blue ink and is illegible.
In entry C, 'in dem' is corrected to 'in einem Rationalitätsbereiche'; the struck word after 'wenn sie' is illegible.

In the AM–GM entry the struck symbols before 'n Zahlen' and after 'arithmetische' are deleted fragments. The last line reads '(a_1+…+a_{2n})/n ≧ ⁿ√(a_1…a_n) + ⁿ√(a_{n+1}…a_{2n}) ≧ 2·√(ⁿ√…·ⁿ√…)  q.e.d.'
